--- title: "Using APIs" format: live-html: theme: - cosmo - brand toc: true css: /styles.css webr: render-df: reactable packages: - dplyr - tidyr resources: - data engine: knitr reference-location: margin citation-location: margin --- In this session, we will be be using 3rd party APIs to retrieve data and expand our dataset. We will be using two services that have public APIs and will be using them via web browser and code. ## Slides ```{=html} ``` [Open the slides in full screen](/content/week_7/slides.html) ## Taginfo From OSM Wiki: > **Taginfo** is a system for finding and aggregating information about OSM tags and making it browsable and searchable. It was created by [Jochen Topf](https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/User:Joto "User:Joto"). > > You can try it out at: [**taginfo.openstreetmap.org**](https://taginfo.openstreetmap.org/). This is the main taginfo site and covers the whole **Why is this useful?** OpenStreetMap uses a system of [^1] (combinations of keys and values) to describe geographic objects. Anyone can create new tags and add them to existing or new objects, making the map very flexible but also potentially confusing. [^1]: Refer to for more information about what tags are and how they work. **How can this help?** Taginfo provides data to adress questions such as: 1. How popular is a tag? How has this changed over time? 2. Where is it used? 3. What does it mean? How to use it? 1. Points, areas... 2. Is it used along other keys 3. Which are the possible values allowed? ### GUI Accessing [**taginfo.openstreetmap.org**](https://taginfo.openstreetmap.org/). ![A screenshot from taginfo, displaying information about a given key (`building`)](media/building-Keys-OpenStreetMap-Taginfo.png){#fig-taginfo-overview} ::: callout-caution ## Task 1. Pick a key (or a tag) of your interest 2. Use the GUI to explore what it says about the them. 3. Can you answer any of the aforementioned questions about the tag? ::: ### API Taginfo offers several endpoints. Each endpoint (and the parameters is accepting and the outputs) is documented here: . As seen in @fig-taginfo-api-documentation, there are multiple endpoints. Each of them is thoroughly described. ![Screenshot of Taginfo's API documentation](media/API-Documentation-OpenStreetMap-Taginfo.png){#fig-taginfo-api-documentation} ::: callout-important #### How to read this? Taginfo's API documentation may seem daunting, but it provides key information that is important to understand: - `path`: is the url of the endpoint that we need to query - `description`: provides an explanation of what the endpoint does - `format`: explains the format in which the results are returned. In this case is a `json` file, which does not store information in rows and columns, and will need to be converted to a data frame. - `paging`: in this case is set to `no`, which means that all the results will be displayed in a single page/file. - `sort`: there's no sorting - `result`: this lists every field contanined in the resulting json file, along with an explanation of their type and a description. - `example`: this provides a URL with a query. This is useful in two ways: 1) we can see the URL patterns, 2) we can see how a result would look like. - `UI example`: the equivalent query, as seen through the GUI (Website). ::: #### Quering Taginfo API with R We will be using two packages: 1. `{jsonlite}`: to work with data stored in a json file. 2. `{dplyr}`: to manipulate a dataframe. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(dplyr) library(jsonlite) selected_key <- "wheelchair" # Set up the API endpoints URL endpoint_chronology <- paste0( "https://taginfo.openstreetmap.org/api/4/key/chronology?key=", selected_key ) # Send a GET request to the API endpoint response <- fromJSON(endpoint_chronology, simplifyDataFrame = TRUE) # Save the data in the response (json) into a dataframe key_chronology <- as.data.frame(response$data) # We want to store the name of the key key_chronology <- key_chronology |> mutate( key = selected_key, date = as.Date(date) ) |> relocate(key, .before = 1) head(key_chronology) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` key date nodes ways relations 1 wheelchair 2007-10-07 0 1 0 2 wheelchair 2007-10-26 0 1 0 3 wheelchair 2008-01-11 2 0 0 4 wheelchair 2008-01-12 12 0 0 5 wheelchair 2008-01-18 0 1 0 6 wheelchair 2008-02-04 2 0 0 ``` ::: ::: We can even create some (basic) visualisations with that data: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Plot cumulative way usage with base R: plot(x = key_chronology$date, y = cumsum(key_chronology$ways), type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "red", main = paste0("Cumulative '", selected_key, "' key usage on ways"), xlab = "Date", ylab = "Ways (cumulative)" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: callout-caution ### Your turn Can you adapt the code to retrieve data from the [prevalent values endpoint](https://taginfo.openstreetmap.org/taginfo/apidoc#api_4_key_prevalent_values)? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} selected_key <- "wheelchair" # Set up the API endpoints URL endpoint_prevalent_values <- paste0( "https://taginfo.openstreetmap.org/api/4/key/prevalent_values?key=", selected_key ) # Retrieve key overview response <- fromJSON(endpoint_prevalent_values, simplifyDataFrame = TRUE) key_prevalent_values <- as.data.frame(response$data) head(key_prevalent_values) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` value count fraction 1 yes 2498034 0.6153 2 no 1026514 0.2529 3 limited 496817 0.1224 4 38181 0.0094 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Overpass Overpass is a read only API that retrieves **map features** containing a certain `key` or `tag`. It offers a way to query the map to look for specific features. You can read more about it in the wiki: ### GUI Probably, the most popular way to intertact with overpass is through the web interface ![Overpass-turbo screenshot displaying features containing `artwork = *` in Warwick's campus](media/overpass-turbo.png){#fig-overpass-turbo} How to use it? Overpass-turbo has a great documemntation in the "help" button, but a possible outline for basic usage could be: 1. Select the region you want to query the features, either by: 1. Navigating the map until the desired area 2. Typing the name of the location in the search box within the map 2. Use the wizard to build your query and providing keys (and optionally, values) ::: callout-tip ### Queries The Wizard builds Overpass queries from a short search expression. It understands the following conditions: Tag conditions - `key=value` — objects tagged key=value - `key!=value` — objects not tagged key=value - `key=*` — objects that have the tag key, with any value - `key!=*` — objects that do not have the tag key - `key~value` — objects whose key value matches a regular expression (append /i to ignore case) - `~key~value` — objects where both the key and the value match a regular expression - `key!~value` — objects whose key value does not match a regular expression - `key:value` — objects whose key value contains value - `value` — a plain search term is looked up among the known presets, e.g. “Drinking Water” ::: 3. Run the query by either: 1. Clicking on "Build and run the query" (on the wizard) 2. Clicking on "Run" (main screen) 4. (optionallly) Export the results ### API Overpass API's documentation is spread across multiple pages at OSM wiki: . #### Quering Taginfo API with R In this case, due to its relatively complexity, we will be using a specialised package to use Overpass API: [`{osmdata}`](https://docs.ropensci.org/osmdata/). ::: callout-tip #### How to get a bounding box coordinates Overpass needs a bounding box (usually shortened to bbox) is a rectangular area defined by two longitudes and two latitudes, where: - Latitude is a decimal number between -90.0 and 90.0. - Longitude is a decimal number between -180.0 and 180.0. They usually follow the standard format of: - bbox = left,bottom,right,top - bbox = min Longitude , min Latitude , max Longitude , max Latitude There are a number of websites to obtain the actual values for a given region, such as ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Uncomment below if you don't have osmdata installed in your system: # install.packages("osmdata") library(osmdata) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Data (c) OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL 1.0. https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright connected to: https://maps.mail.ru/osm/tools/overpass/api/interpreter ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Getting our bounding box warwick_bbox <- getbb ("University of Warwick") #warwick_bbox <- c(-1.57418,52.37887,-1.55783,52.38314) #Obtained from https://norbertrenner.de/osm/bbox.html # See which server you're using get_overpass_url() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "https://maps.mail.ru/osm/tools/overpass/api/interpreter" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Switch to a mirror set_overpass_url("https://overpass-api.de/api/interpreter") warwick_art <- opq(bbox = warwick_bbox) |> add_osm_feature(key = "tourism", value = "artwork") |> osmdata_sf() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Waiting 14.9998378753662 seconds ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Explore the data warwick_art ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Object of class 'osmdata' with: $bbox : 52.3706939,-1.5773781,52.3913551,-1.5490306 $overpass_call : The call submitted to the overpass API $meta : metadata including timestamp and version numbers $osm_points : 'sf' Simple Features Collection with 19 points $osm_lines : NULL $osm_polygons : 'sf' Simple Features Collection with 0 polygons $osm_multilines : NULL $osm_multipolygons : NULL ``` ::: ::: ::: aside `sf` stands for [Simple Features](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/), and is a data type used to store geospatial information. Geospatial features can be: - points - lines - polygons (i.e., closed shapes) - multilines (a group of lines, not necessarily adjacent) - multipolygons (a group of polygons, not necessarily adjacent) Refer to for more information. ::: ::: callout-important #### Understanding osmdata objects The `warwick_art` returned by our query is a list that contains multiple nested objects: - `$bbox`: the bounding box containing the features - `$overpass_call`: the call made to overpass api, using overpass syntax - `$meta`: medatada - `$osm_points`: a `sf` object containing points - `$osm_lines`: a `sf` object containing lines - `$osm_polygons`: a `sf` object containing polygons - `$osm_multilines`: a `sf` object containing multilines - `$osm_multipolygons`: a `sf` object containing multipolygons For more information, refer to ::: #### Creating a map Let's explore the actual data from overpass: ::: {.cell .column-page} ```{.r .cell-code} head(warwick_art$osm_points) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` osm_id name artist_name 2502341718 2502341718 3B Series No 1 Bernard Schottlander 4951142727 4951142727 Let's Not Be Stupid Richard Deacon 5065989300 5065989300 Needle of Knowledge Obelisk Stefan Knapp 5081993647 5081993647 5428430940 5428430940 Days of Judgement - Cat 1 5428430941 5428430941 Butterworth Bench artwork:material artwork_type heritage 2502341718 welded mild steel painted bright red sculpture 2 4951142727 sculpture 5065989300 5081993647 5428430940 sculpture 5428430941 heritage:operator listed_status source start_date tourism 2502341718 Historic England Grade II bing 1968 artwork 4951142727 artwork 5065989300 survery artwork 5081993647 survery artwork 5428430940 artwork 5428430941 artwork geometry 2502341718 -1.56067, 52.37792 4951142727 -1.562199, 52.378942 5065989300 -1.56396, 52.38194 5081993647 -1.560694, 52.380967 5428430940 -1.562934, 52.379493 5428430941 -1.560258, 52.380195 ``` ::: ::: As we can see, this object contains both, geometry, and attributes describing the feature ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"} ### Can you recognise any of those attributes? Indeed! Each of the column names are different keys from OpenStreetMap! ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Uncomment below if you don't have osmdata installed in your system: # install.packages("leaflet") library(leaflet) # Save into a separate object to reduce typing. points <- warwick_art$osm_points # Create the interactive map leaflet() |> addTiles() |> addMarkers(data = points) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: We can do slightly better by adding some popups displaying the attributes: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # We create a new column aggregating multiple fields to be displayed in the popup points <- points |> mutate( popup = paste( sep = "
", name, artist_name, artwork_type ) ) # Now, repeat the map, but adding labels and a popup leaflet() |> addTiles() |> addMarkers( data = points, label = ~name, popup = ~popup ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Wrap up In this session we've learnt a number of different things! 1. We got a theoretical understanding on strategies to work with big data. 1. And how API's are examples of outscaling our infrastructure 2. Through interacting with two different API services we learnt: 1. We gained an understanding on how to get started with API services (e.g. documentation) and what to expect from them 2. We learnt how to interact via GUI and through code 3. When interacting with API through code, we learnt: 1. To use generic functions to query the APIs directly 2. To use specialised libraries to work with specific APIs And we have also refreshed concepts from previous week: 1. Manipulating data using `dplyr`.
